title: Replace combinational 32-bit divider with a stalling radix-2 iterative divider
motivation:
Baseline Fmax is 5.44 MHz with a 199.8 ns / 150-logic-level worst path
(u_mem.rd -> u_fwd -> u_ex -> u_ex/u_alu -> dmem). That depth, and most of the
12.3k LUT4s, comes from the combinational `/` and `%` in alu.sv: Gowin builds
DIV, DIVU, REM and REMU as chains of 32 subtract-and-compare stages. Fitness is
CoreMark/MHz (~2.23) x Fmax, so the divider sets the clock for every other
instruction. CoreMark -O3 runs almost no divides inside the timed window
(list, matrix, state and crc kernels use shifts, adds and muls). Making the
divider multi-cycle should cost almost no cycles and remove a path that is
roughly 5-10x longer than any other path in the core.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Remove DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU from the combinational ALU and run them on a small
sequential divider in EX: restoring, radix-2, one quotient bit per cycle,
about 33-34 cycles per divide. Sign is handled outside the loop. The divider
holds the pipeline with the existing stall mechanism.

Divider (new rtl/divider.sv):
  - On start, latch the raw post-forward operands a_q/b_q (rs1/rs2 as seen
    in EX on the first cycle), is_signed, and want_rem. Load the magnitudes
    |a| and |b| (take |x| only for signed ops) into a 32-bit remainder
    register, a 32-bit dividend/quotient shift register and a 32-bit divisor
    register. Each cycle does one 33-bit trial subtract and one shift. A
    6-bit counter drives `done`.
  - Final fixup: quotient negate = signed && (a[31]^b[31]) && (b != 0);
    remainder negate = signed && a[31]. Restoring division gives
    q = all-ones and r = a for b == 0, and the INT_MIN / -1 overflow case
    becomes q = 0x80000000, r = 0. Both match RV32M with no special-case
    compare in the loop. Register the fixed-up result, so the output mux
    only adds one 2:1 level to EX.
  - Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS`: the result is the same ALTOPS
    formula as today ((a_q - b_q) ^ const per op), computed from the
    latched operands, and latency drops to 1-2 cycles. Formal still
    covers the start, stall, operand-latch and complete handshake inside
    the BMC depth, and the liveness check stays short.

Pipeline integration:
  - div_busy = ID/EX.valid && is_div_op && !div_done. While it is high:
    stall_if = 1; stall_id = 1 (hold, no flush; a divide never redirects);
    EX/MEM takes a bubble (valid=0, reg_write=0, mem_read=mem_write=0,
    is_illegal=0) so forward_unit and ex_mem_mem_op see nothing.
    MEM/WB keeps draining normally. dmem_stall keeps priority: if it is
    active, EX/MEM holds as today and the divider may keep iterating.
  - Latch the operands only on the start cycle. After that, the older
    producers leave EX/MEM and MEM/WB, so forwarding would return stale
    ID/EX.rs?_val.
  - On done, EX's alu_result mux picks div_result, and EX/MEM captures the
    divide normally with rs1_val/rs2_val taken from the latched a_q/b_q so
    RVFI rs?_rdata stay exact. `done` clears on the cycle EX/MEM captures
    (!stall_ex_mem).
  - Add an is_div flag to ctrl_t, or decode it from alu_op range 15..18.

Expected effect: the worst path moves to the forward-mux -> DSP multiplier
or forward -> branch compare -> redirect -> PC -> imem path, likely
25-45 MHz instead of 5.4. CoreMark/MHz should be within about 1% of today.
Net fitness gain should be several hundred percent, far above the 4.6%
acceptance bar. LUT4 count should drop sharply (~12.3k -> ~3-4k).

changes.description: New sequential radix-2 restoring divider. Latches operands on start, runs about 33 cycles, fixes up sign, registers the result. Handles RV32M div-by-0 and overflow cases. Under RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS it returns the ALTOPS formula from the latched operands with 1-2 cycle latency.
Delete the combinational / and % arms (DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU give 0 or don't-care; the real result comes from divider.sv). Keep MUL* and the ALTOPS MUL* arms unchanged.

Instantiate divider. Start it when ID/EX holds a valid div op that is not active or done. Add a div_busy output. Mux div_result into alu_result on completion. Put a bubble into EX/MEM while busy (unless dmem-stall hold applies). Record latched operands as rs1_val/rs2_val for a divide's RVFI. Clear done when EX/MEM captures.
Add a div_busy input. It asserts stall_if and stall_id (hold, not flush) and does not flush_id. dmem_stall still has priority for EX/MEM hold. Expose a bubble_ex signal (div_busy && !dmem_stall).
Wire div_busy and bubble_ex between ex_stage and hazard_unit. Top-level IO unchanged.
Optionally add an is_div bit to ctrl_t, or keep decoding it from alu_op (ALU_DIV..ALU_REMU).
If ctrl_t.is_div is added, set it for funct7=0000001 with funct3[2]=1. Illegal-default discipline unchanged.
Remove the combinational DIV/REM checks from the ALU test, since the ALU no longer computes them. Keep all MUL/base-op vectors.

New cocotb test for the clocked divider: port all existing DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU vectors (div-by-zero, INT_MIN/-1, sign mixes, random) plus back-to-back ops. Each check pulses start, waits for done and compares the exact bit result.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r1s0 (regression, +739.85%): Making only DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU a stalling radix-2 sequential unit took Fmax from ~5.4 to ~45 MHz at negligible CoreMark IPC cost, since the combinational `/`/`%` was nearly the whole critical path; it is labelled a regression only because sibling r1s1 also moved MUL into the multi-cycle unit and scored ~1.4% higher, which is inside the ~6% seed spread, so the DSP multiplier is not a significant next Fmax limiter.

title: Move MUL/DIV/REM out of the 1-cycle EX ALU into a multi-cycle stalling M-unit
motivation:
The baseline runs at 5.44 MHz: the worst path (199.8 ns, 156 logic cells) is
MEM/WB.rd -> forward_unit -> EX operand mux -> alu.sv -> EX/MEM (-> dmem BSRAM
address register). That depth is the fully combinational 32-bit `/` and `%`
(signed + unsigned, i.e. four ripple-array dividers) sitting in the single-cycle
EX stage, plus three separate 64-bit multipliers (ss/uu/su, 6 DSPs). Everything
else in the 5-stage pipe (forward mux, 32-bit add/compare, redirect) is ~10-15
LUT levels, so the pipeline is ~10x slower than it has to be because of
instructions that are nearly absent from the CoreMark timed loop: essentially no
DIV/REM, and ~1.6k MULs per iteration (N=9 matrix kernels: 729*2 + 81*4) against
~449k cycles/iteration. Taking M-ext arithmetic off the single-cycle path costs
well under 1% IPC and should buy an order of magnitude in Fmax. It also removes
most of the 12.3k LUT4s (the dividers dominate area).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure EX into a 1-cycle integer ALU plus a separate multi-cycle M-unit
(rtl/mdu.sv) with a start/busy/done handshake that stalls the front of the pipe.

1. alu.sv keeps only the RV32I ops (ADD..LUI). The M-ext arms (both the real
   and the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS branch) move into mdu.sv. No `/`, `%` or `*`
   remains on the EX combinational path.

2. mdu.sv (new):
   - Launch: when ID/EX holds a valid M-op and the unit is idle, latch op and
     the POST-FORWARD rs1/rs2 values (the forwarding sources are correct in
     this cycle exactly as for a normal ALU op).
   - Multiply: one shared 33x33 signed multiplier (operands sign- or
     zero-extended per MUL/MULH/MULHSU/MULHU) replacing the three 64-bit
     products; input registers -> product register (maps onto Gowin DSP
     internal pipeline regs), then low/high-half select. ~3-cycle latency.
   - Divide: radix-2 restoring divider on operand magnitudes, 1 quotient bit
     per cycle (32 iterations) + sign fix-up; RV32M special cases handled at
     launch as an early-out (div-by-0 -> q=all-ones, r=dividend;
     INT_MIN/-1 -> q=INT_MIN, r=0). The iteration datapath is a single 33-bit
     subtract + shift register, i.e. one short carry chain per cycle.
   - Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` the unit uses the same handshake but
     produces the existing ALTOPS formulas with a short fixed latency (1-2
     cycles), so riscv-formal still exercises the stall/launch/complete
     control within its 20-step BMC depth while real arithmetic stays out of
     the solver.
   - done/result are held until EX/MEM actually captures them (a dmem stall
     may freeze EX/MEM in the completion cycle).

3. Pipeline control (hazard_unit.sv / core.sv / ex_stage.sv):
   - mdu_stall = ID/EX is a valid M-op && !mdu_done. While asserted:
     stall_if = stall_id = 1 (PC and ID/EX hold, no flush), and EX/MEM
     captures a bubble (valid=0, reg_write=0, mem_read/mem_write=0) so older
     instructions drain through MEM/WB normally. dmem_stall keeps priority
     (EX/MEM holds). No interaction with redirect (an M-op is never a
     branch/jump) or load-use (ID/EX is not a load).
   - On completion EX/MEM captures the M-op with alu_result = mdu result, and
     rs1_val/rs2_val/write_data taken from the MDU's LATCHED operands, not the
     live forward mux (while waiting, the producer may have retired to the
     regfile, making ID/EX.rs?_val stale and the live mux wrong for RVFI).
   - After completion the M-op result forwards from EX/MEM/MEM-WB exactly
     like any ALU result; no forwarding-unit change needed.

4. Tests: add test/test_mdu.py (clocked cocotb) carrying every M-ext vector
   from test_alu.py (exact bit results incl. div-by-zero, INT_MIN/-1,
   MULHSU sign cases, back-to-back ops); test_alu.py keeps the RV32I vectors.
   test_pipeline.py gains a back-to-back dependent MUL->DIV->ADD sequence
   and an M-op followed by a load-use and a taken branch.

MEASURED PROBE (make timing TARGET=bench, place option 0, hypgen worktree,
reverted afterwards): with only the four DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU arms stubbed to
0 in alu.sv (MUL still combinational), Gowin reports Fmax 49.08 MHz (vs
5.44), logic 2071 LUTs (vs 12312), 17 logic levels. The new top paths are
all ~25.6 ns and tied: (a) regfile LUTRAM -> ID -> EX -> IF redirect ->
hazard -> ID/EX.rs2_val (redirect/flush path), and (b) regfile -> EX ->
alu (multiplier) -> EX/MEM -> dmem BSRAM address. So the divider alone is
worth ~9x Fmax; pipelining the multiplier (step 2) takes path (b) out of the
tie and saves 4-5 DSPs, but the ceiling is then set by the redirect path.
Implementation constraint so this ceiling is not lost: mdu_stall must be
derived from REGISTERED state (ID/EX.ctrl.is_mdu && ID/EX.valid &&
!mdu_done_q), never from the forward mux or MDU datapath, because it
feeds stall_if/stall_id alongside the already-critical redirect/hazard
logic.

Expected: Fmax ~45-50 MHz (probe value minus a little for the MDU
handshake), CoreMark/MHz drops <1% (≈1.6k MULs x 2-3 extra cycles + a
handful of DIV/REM x ~33 cycles per 449k-cycle iteration). Fitness
≈ 2.2 CoreMark/MHz x ~48 MHz ≈ 100 iter/s, ~8x the 12.12 champion (the
schema caps the field below at +50). LUT4 count falls to ~2.2k, well
below the 10k target.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r1s1 (improvement, +752.15%): Once DIV/REM and MUL are both in a stalling M-unit, Fmax stops near the ~49 MHz probe ceiling set by the regfile LUTRAM -> EX branch compare -> redirect -> hazard -> ID/EX flush path (~25.6 ns, 17 levels), so moving MUL off EX adds almost nothing; later Fmax work has to shorten redirect/flush, and new stall signals such as mdu_stall must come only from registered ID/EX + done-flop state so they do not lengthen that path.

title: Zero-bubble fetch-stage branch prediction: predecode + 256-entry bimodal BHT, predicted JAL
motivation:
Fmax is pinned at ~5.4 MHz by the combinational divider path
(fwd -> EX -> ALU, ~200 ns). Logic outside that path does not affect
Fmax, so this hypothesis can only move fitness through IPC, and any
IPC gain maps 1:1 onto fitness.

Every taken control transfer currently costs one fetch slot. Control
flow resolves in EX; the instruction fetched behind it (pc+4) is
flushed and the target is fetched one cycle later. I measured this on
the exact scored binary (-O3, TOTAL_DATA_SIZE=2000, ITERATIONS=10)
with test/cosim/reference.py, between the 0x10000100 and 0x10000104
markers:
  - 2,922,016 retired instructions (~292k per iteration). The champion
    spends 5.442e6/12.12 = ~449k cycles per iteration (CPI ~1.54).
  - 529,588 conditional branches (294,425 taken; 235,191 of the taken
    ones are backward), 49,367 JAL, 13,735 JALR (all returns).
  - That is 357,527 redirect bubbles, ~35.8k per iteration = ~8.0% of
    all cycles.
Because IF/ID is combinational (the instruction is decoded in the same
cycle it is fetched), a predictor placed there can steer the very next
fetch and remove the bubble completely for correct predictions.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a fetch-stage direction predictor and a predecoded target, and
make EX redirect only on mispredictions.

1. IF predecode (raw io_imemData, not the flushed/NOP'd copy, so
   redirect isn't on this path): detect BRANCH (opcode 1100011) and JAL
   (1101111), build the B/J immediate, target = pc + imm (one 32-bit
   adder; the J/B imm mux feeds it).
     - JAL: pred_taken = 1.
     - BRANCH: pred_taken = BHT[pc[9:2]][1].
     - Never predict taken if imm[1] = 1 (misaligned target). The
       existing EX misalign-trap path (no redirect, pc_next = pc+4)
       then stays consistent with the prediction.
     - JALR: not predicted, and it still redirects exactly as today.
       A 4-entry return stack would only recover 13.7k bubbles
       (~0.35%) and would put a 32-bit target compare on the redirect
       path, so it is deliberately out of scope.
2. BHT: 256 x 2-bit saturating counters indexed by pc[9:2]. Reset or
   initialize them to weakly-taken (2'b10). Flops or LUT-RAM are both
   fine. The BHT only affects performance, never architectural state,
   so uninitialized contents are still correct for formal. It is
   updated from EX when the ID/EX instruction is a valid branch and
   !stall_ex_mem (a branch held by a dmem stall is counted once), using
   the resolved branch condition and the ID/EX pc[9:2].
3. if_stage next-PC priority: redirect -> redirect_target; else stall
   -> hold; else pred_taken -> pred_target; else pc+4. io_imemAddr is
   still the PC register. PC advances through a prediction exactly
   when the IF instruction is captured into ID/EX (imem stall,
   load-use and dmem stall all hold the PC), so no wrong-path
   instruction ever carries a stale prediction.
4. Carry pred_taken through if_id_t and id_ex_t. It must be 0 for
   flushed/invalid IF output, and ID/EX flush zeroes it. In EX:
     actual_taken = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault
                    (today's redirect expression)
     redirect        = (actual_taken != pred_taken) || (is_jalr && actual_taken)
     redirect_target = actual_taken ? (is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target)
                                    : pc + 4
   A predicted-taken branch or JAL always has the correct target
   (pc+imm), so no target compare is needed. pc_next / RVFI stay
   EX-resolved as today, so pc_fwd/pc_bwd, unique, liveness and ill
   checks see the same architectural stream. flush_if/flush_id on
   redirect are unchanged.

Trace-driven estimate on the scored binary: with all JALs and BHT-hit
branches bubble-free, the remaining bubbles are 44,293 branch
mispredicts (256-entry bimodal; 64 entries gives 51,419 and 512 gives
39,814) plus 13,735 JALRs = 58,028, down from 357,527. That saves
~30.0k of ~449k cycles per iteration (-6.7% cycles, +7.1% iter/cycle).
By comparison, static BTFN+JAL only recovers ~5.2% of cycles, too
close to the 4.6% acceptance bar, which is why this uses a dynamic
BHT. The added paths are pc reg -> BHT read -> PC mux and imem data ->
imm -> adder -> PC mux (roughly 15-20 ns), and the fwd -> branch
compare -> BHT write. All of them are far shorter than the 200 ns
divider path, so Fmax should stay within P&R noise.

changes.description: New module. Combinational predecode of the raw fetched word (BRANCH/JAL detect, B/J immediate, pc+imm target adder, suppress when imm[1]=1). 256x2-bit bimodal BHT read at pc[9:2] (weakly-taken init). Synchronous update port (en, idx=ex_pc[9:2], taken) with saturating increment/decrement. Outputs pred_taken and pred_target.

Instantiate branch_predictor. next_pc = redirect ? redirect_target : stall ? pc : pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4. Export pred_taken in the IF/ID bundle, forced to 0 whenever out.valid is 0 (flush/redirect). Pass the BHT update port through from core.
Add a 'pred_taken' bit to if_id_t and id_ex_t.
Latch in.pred_taken into ID/EX alongside the other fields (reset/flush zeroes it).

Redirect only on misprediction. actual_taken = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault. redirect = (actual_taken != in.pred_taken) || (is_jalr && actual_taken). redirect_target = actual_taken ? Wire the EX BHT update signals into if_stage/branch_predictor. No IO or RVFI changes.

title: Valid-bit squash pipeline control: take EX redirect off the fetch/decode/regfile/flush path
motivation:
The champion (r1s1, 48.3 MHz, 103.28 iter/s) is limited by a single
structural path, not by arithmetic. Timing reports it as regfile LUTRAM /
ID/EX -> EX forward mux -> 32-bit branch compare -> redirect -> if_stage NOP
mux -> regfile read address + hazard load-use compare -> stall_id/flush_id
-> clock-enable / sync-reset of all ~180 ID/EX flops (19 levels, 26.8 ns).
The chain exists only because the pipeline squashes wrong-path work by
*rewriting data*. A taken branch in EX (1) forces the combinational IF/ID
instruction to a NOP. That NOP then feeds the decoder, the regfile read
addresses, the regfile write-first bypass compare and the load-use compare.
(2) It also drives flush_id, a synchronous reset on every ID/EX bit.
stall_id (the ID/EX clock enable) also depends on load_use, which depends
on the NOP-muxed rs1/rs2. So the branch compare feeds the regfile read and
a high-fanout CE/reset net. None of that is architecturally needed: a
squashed instruction only has to be *invalid*, not zero.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Change pipeline control from "flush by zeroing registers" to "squash by
clearing valid bits". The EX redirect then drives only the PC mux and one
ID/EX.valid flop. A taken branch still squashes the same single
wrong-path fetch slot, and no stage is added, so CoreMark cycle count is
unchanged.

1. if_stage: remove the `(flush||redirect) ? NOP : imem_data` mux. out.instr
   = io_imemData always, and out.valid = imem_ready (the valid bit no longer
   depends on redirect). The PC register logic stays the same (redirect >
   stall > pc+4).
2. id_stage / reg_file: the decoder, imm_gen, the regfile read addresses and
   the ID/EX rs?_addr/rd fields all take the raw instruction. The ID/EX
   register has no reset-on-flush for data fields. Its clock enable is
   `!(dmem_stall || mdu_stall)`, which depends only on registered state and
   the stall-gen input, not on redirect or load_use. Only the valid bit sees
   the squash:
   valid_d = in.valid && !redirect && !load_use_hazard. On load-use, ID/EX
   captures a garbage copy of the dependent instruction with valid=0, and
   the PC holds, so the same instruction is presented again next cycle.
   That matches today's bubble behaviour.
3. hazard_unit: load_use = id_ex.valid && id_ex.mem_read && rd!=0 &&
   (rd == imem_data[19:15] || rd == imem_data[24:20]), using the raw fetched
   word. This is safe because (a) redirect and load_use cannot both be true
   (ID/EX holds either a LOAD or a branch/jump), and redirect still takes
   priority on the PC, and (b) during an imem stall the IF slot is invalid
   anyway and the PC holds. A spurious match only re-captures an invalid
   slot. stall_if = load_use || imem_stall || dmem_stall || mdu_stall
   (unchanged). flush_id and flush_if are removed.
4. ex_stage: qualify every side effect with in.valid at the point it is
   captured into EX/MEM, not on the critical path. That covers
   reg_write/mem_read/mem_write/is_illegal/is_mdu in ctrl, and redirect =
   in.valid && (taken||jump) && !misalign. mdu_stall already uses in.valid.
   The EX/MEM bubble on mdu_stall can also become valid=0 with ctrl side
   effects cleared, instead of a full '0 reset. The forward_unit then sees
   reg_write already qualified by validity. MEM/WB keeps its hold_wb
   semantics unchanged.
5. Optional, only if the post-change timing report still shows the
   forward-select compare at the head of the path: register the
   forward-mux selects one cycle early in ID, and hold them on dmem_stall.
   Select EX/MEM for the new ID/EX when the current ID/EX is valid and
   writes that rd. Otherwise select MEM/WB when the current EX/MEM writes
   it. This does not change the data forwarding the EX stage uses. MDU ops
   still latch operands on their first cycle.
6. Dedicated address adder. Gowin absorbs the EX/MEM address register into
   the dmem BSRAM read-address register (the baseline's worst path ended at
   dmem_0_dmem_0_0_0_s). That means the whole ALU (barrel shifter + 11-way
   op mux + jump/mdu mux) currently sits in front of BSRAM address setup.
   Add an EX/MEM field mem_addr = rs1_fwd + imm (its own 32-bit adder, no op
   mux). Drive io_dmemAddr, byte_mask, misalign and load-shift from it in
   mem_stage. alu_result keeps feeding forwarding and writeback as today.
   For every load/store the value is identical.

-> PC mux, or ID/EX -> forward mux -> ALU -> EX/MEM / dmem BSRAM address.

architectural-state write is still gated by valid bits, so RVFI ordering
and trap semantics are preserved.

title: Fetch-stage bimodal predictor with a registered (one-cycle-late) mispredict redirect to take branch resolution off the critical path
motivation:
The champion (r1s1, 48.3 MHz, 103.28) is limited by one combinational chain
(~25.6-26.8 ns, 17-19 levels): ID/EX -> forward mux -> 32-bit branch compare
in EX -> `redirect` -> if_stage NOP mux on out.instr -> regfile read address
and hazard_unit load-use compare -> stall/flush of the ID/EX register
(endpoint id_ex.rs1_val). The redirect has to be combinational today because
the core predicts not-taken: every taken branch/JAL/JALR costs a bubble, and
deferring the redirect by one cycle would make that 2 bubbles.

Measured on the scored binary (r1s2, reference.py trace): 529,588
conditional branches (294,425 taken), 49,367 JAL, 13,735 JALR, which is
357.5k redirect bubbles out of ~4.68M timed cycles (~7.6%). r1s2's fetch
predictor (predecoded pc+imm, 256x2b bimodal, JAL always taken) removed
~298k of them. That puts conditional mispredicts at ~45k, so after the
predictor only ~59k control transfers per run (mispredicts + JALR) still
need a redirect.

With a predictor in place, redirects are rare. The redirect can then come
from a flop one cycle later and still cost far fewer cycles than today. That
removes the EX compare -> IF/hazard/ID-flush chain that sets Fmax.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Port the r1s2 fetch predictor to the champion. Resolve mispredicts in EX
but act on them from a register in the next cycle, so no EX result
combinationally drives the PC, IF/ID, the hazard unit or the ID/EX enables.

1. Fetch predictor (new rtl/branch_predictor.sv, used by if_stage). Predecode
   the RAW io_imemData (never the NOP-muxed copy): BRANCH (1100011) and
   JAL (1101111), B/J immediate, pred_target = pc + imm (one 32-bit adder).
   JAL is always predicted taken. BRANCH is predicted from a 256 x 2-bit
   bimodal counter table indexed by pc[9:2] (flops or LUT-RAM, weakly-taken
   init). Never predict taken when imm[1]=1 (misaligned target); EX's
   misalign trap then stays unchanged. JALR is not predicted. Carry
   pred_taken and the 2-bit counter value read at fetch through
   if_id_t/id_ex_t, so EX computes the saturating update without a second
   table read port. pred_taken must be 0 whenever out.valid=0.
   next_pc priority: redirect_q ? ex_mem.pc_next : stall_if ? pc :
   pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4.

2. EX resolves, EX/MEM remembers. In ex_stage:
     actual_taken = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault
     mispredict   = in.valid && !kill && (actual_taken != in.pred_taken)
   No target compare is needed: a predicted-taken branch/JAL used exactly
   pc+imm, which equals EX's branch_target/jump_target. JALR always
   mispredicts because pred_taken=0. Register `mispredict` into a new EX/MEM
   field (only when EX/MEM captures, i.e. !stall_ex_mem && !mdu_stall).
   The redirect target is the existing EX/MEM.pc_next, which is already the
   architecturally correct next PC including the misalign fallback, so no
   new target mux sits in EX. Remove the combinational `redirect` /
   `redirect_target` outputs.

3. Kill in the cycle after (kill = redirect_q = EX/MEM.valid &&
   EX/MEM.mispredict, a flop). Two wrong-path instructions are in flight: W1
   in ID/EX (being executed) and W2 in fetch.
     - PC <- EX/MEM.pc_next (overrides every stall, as redirect does today).
     - ID/EX captures a bubble (flush_id = kill || (load_use && !dmem_stall)).
     - EX/MEM captures a bubble for W1 (same arm as mdu_stall, reg_q <= '0).
       Gate W1's mispredict, BHT update and MDU start with !kill, and gate
       mdu_stall with !kill, so a wrong-path M-op never starts or holds the
       pipe.
   A dmem stall cannot coincide with kill: the branch/jump is the
   instruction in EX/MEM and it has no memory op. So redirect_q is a clean
   one-cycle pulse. Wrong-path instructions never reach MEM, so they cannot
   write dmem or the regfile, and RVFI never sees them. The retiring branch
   already reports pc_wdata = pc_next.

4. Timing clean-ups that come for free. if_stage stops muxing NOP into
   out.instr. The regfile read addresses and hazard_unit's load-use rs1/rs2
   come from raw io_imemData, with validity carried only in the valid bit and
   the flushes. flush_if becomes imem_stall || kill (all flop-sourced). After
   this, every PC / ID/EX control input comes from flops plus the short
   imem_data -> load-use compare. The EX branch compare only feeds EX/MEM D
   inputs (~9-10 levels, about the same as the fwd -> ALU -> EX/MEM path).

Expected cycles: bubbles go from 357.5k (1 per taken transfer) to about
2 x (45k cond mispredicts + 13.7k JALR) = ~118k. That saves ~240k of
~4.68M cycles, about +5% IPC (r1s2's model matched measurement within
0.5 pp). Expected Fmax: the new worst path should be ID/EX -> fwd mux -> ALU
-> EX/MEM, or the fetch predecode -> pc+imm adder -> PC mux. Both are
roughly 10-12 levels vs today's 17-19, so about 58-63 MHz (+20-30%).
Combined estimate is +20-35%, conservatively +22%.
